Random covariance matrices

Source: R/random_covariance.R
random_covariance.Rd

Draws random covariance matrices for simulations: a random correlation matrix scaled by a vector of variances. Correlations come from the LKJ distribution used as a prior by lmm_animal, from the partial-correlation construction of evolqg::RandomMatrix(), or from a two-regime model that combines a positive size axis with a sign-oriented random LKJ residual.

Usage

random_covariance(
  n_traits,
  n_matrices = 1,
  variances = NULL,
  min_var = 1,
  max_var = 1,
  method = c("lkj", "partial", "factor"),
  lkj_prior = 2,
  integration = NULL,
  trait_names = NULL
)

Arguments

n_traits

Number of traits, a whole number of at least 1.

n_matrices

Number of matrices to draw, a whole number of at least 1.

variances

Optional vector of variances, one per trait, with finite positive values. The default draws them uniformly between min_var and max_var.

min_var, max_var

Bounds of the uniform distribution of variances when variances is NULL: finite positive numbers with min_var not above max_var.

method

Correlation model. "lkj" (default) draws a correlation matrix from the LKJ distribution with shape lkj_prior; "partial" draws partial correlations uniformly, reproducing evolqg::RandomMatrix(); "factor" combines a positive size factor with a sign-oriented random LKJ residual, so PC1 is a size axis and draws differ at a fixed integration level.

lkj_prior

LKJ shape for method = "lkj" and for the random residual of method = "factor", a finite number above 0. The default 2 matches the prior of lmm_animal.

integration

For method = "factor", the target integration level, measured as the relative eigenvalue variance of evolqg::CalcEigenVar(rel = TRUE) and so between 0 and 1. A single number targets that level for every matrix; two numbers draw the target uniformly between them. The default NULL draws from 0.1 to 0.8, spanning weak to strong integration. Supplying it with another method is an error.

trait_names

Optional trait names, one per trait; the default is trait1, trait2, ...

Value

With n_matrices = 1, a named symmetric positive-definite matrix. With more than one matrix, a list of such matrices.

Details

The variances are independent of the correlations, and the correlation matrix \(R\) is scaled as \(R \odot \sqrt{v v^T}\), so the diagonal is \(v\). With the default min_var = max_var = 1 the result is a correlation matrix, as in evolqg::RandomMatrix(); using those defaults for both G and E gives a heritability of 0.5 for every trait. Use variances, or a wider min_var/max_var, to vary the heritabilities.

The LKJ method is the default because it matches the prior family of the models and stays well conditioned: correlations are shrunk toward zero by lkj_prior, and a five-trait matrix typically has a condition number in the tens. The partial-correlation method reproduces evolqg::RandomMatrix() and is the one to use when the simulation should span a realistic range of integration: at five traits its first principal component can explain up to about 90% of the variance and the mean squared correlation can approach 0.8, while LKJ(2) stays well below that. The cost is conditioning: the strongly integrated draws often have condition numbers in the hundreds or more, whereas real size-dominated matrices have a single positive axis and can reach the same integration with much smaller condition numbers. Use the partial method to span the range, or deliberately as a hard case for an estimator, not as a neutral default.

Unlike evolqg::RandomMatrix(), this function also handles one and two traits with method = "partial".

With method = "factor" the random part is \(R_{res} = (1 - \delta) I + \delta R_{LKJ}\), where \(R_{LKJ}\) is a random LKJ correlation whose leading eigenvector has been oriented to be positive and \(\delta = 0.3\). Orienting keeps PC1 positive while leaving the remaining components free to carry negative correlations. For targets below the integration of \(R_{res}\), the matrix is \((1 - \alpha) I + \alpha R_{res}\), which shrinks the random structure toward independence without flattening it into equicorrelation. For higher targets the matrix is \(\rho 11^T + (1 - \rho) R_{res}\), which adds the equal-loading size factor; at \(\rho = 1\) it is all ones, whose relative eigenvalue variance is 1. Both regimes have diagonal 1 and are solved to match the requested integration. Because \(R_{LKJ}\) is redrawn for every matrix, draws at a fixed integration differ in their lower components. This is the method to use for size-dominated morphometric simulations: it spans the full integration range while staying far better conditioned than bending an LKJ spectrum directly (at five traits the median condition number is about 4 at 0.1, 16 at 0.5 and 53 at 0.8). At two traits the target fixes the single correlation, so draws at a fixed integration are identical up to the sign orientation.

See also

animal_prior_draws, size_shape

Examples

set.seed(1)
G <- random_covariance(3, min_var = 0.5, max_var = 1.5)
round(G, 2)
#>        trait1 trait2 trait3
#> trait1   0.77   0.51   0.19
#> trait2   0.51   0.87  -0.43
#> trait3   0.19  -0.43   1.07
round(cov2cor(G), 2)
#>        trait1 trait2 trait3
#> trait1   1.00   0.62   0.21
#> trait2   0.62   1.00  -0.44
#> trait3   0.21  -0.44   1.00
eigen(G, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
#> [1] 1.4772680 1.1197192 0.1134987

# Reproduce the evolqg construction
random_covariance(2, n_matrices = 3, method = "partial")
#> [[1]]
#>            trait1     trait2
#> trait1  1.0000000 -0.6468865
#> trait2 -0.6468865  1.0000000
#> 
#> [[2]]
#>           trait1    trait2
#> trait1 1.0000000 0.5396828
#> trait2 0.5396828 1.0000000
#> 
#> [[3]]
#>           trait1    trait2
#> trait1 1.0000000 0.9838122
#> trait2 0.9838122 1.0000000
#> 

# A strongly integrated size axis: PC1 dominates and is positive
S <- random_covariance(5, method = "factor", integration = 0.8)
R <- cov2cor(S)
round(R, 2)
#>        trait1 trait2 trait3 trait4 trait5
#> trait1   1.00   0.90   0.89   0.89   0.91
#> trait2   0.90   1.00   0.90   0.89   0.90
#> trait3   0.89   0.90   1.00   0.87   0.88
#> trait4   0.89   0.89   0.87   1.00   0.90
#> trait5   0.91   0.90   0.88   0.90   1.00
eigen(R, symmetric = TRUE)$vectors[, 1]
#> [1] -0.4493574 -0.4490820 -0.4438025 -0.4448958 -0.4488991
